speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the
text: Minister for Social and Family Development): Mr Speaker, on behalf of the Minister for Social and Family Development, I beg to move, "That the Bill be now read a Second time." Families are the bedrock of our society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the
text: For our children, families are where they first learn the values that shape them, find comfort and strength when they face setbacks and celebrate milestones and achievements together.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As the infographic is being distributed in the House, I would like to highlight that Members will see on the first page of the infographic our comprehensive suite of marriage and parenthood measures to support families.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: And on the second page of the infographic, Members will see our enhancements of parental leave over the years.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Members may also access these materials through the MP@SGPARL app.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Looking at the second page of the infographic, we see that one week of Government-Paid Paternity Leave (GPPL) and one week of Shared Parental Leave (SPL) were first introduced by Minister Grace Fu in January 2013 as part of the 2013 Marriage and Parenthood Package.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: To quote from her speech: "We will signal strongly to the society on the important role fathers play in raising and caring for their children.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Fathers will now enjoy one week of legislated Government-Paid Paternity Leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In addition, we will introduce a new Government-Paid Shared Parental Leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: By inculcating shared parental responsibility from birth, we hope to put families off to a good start and encourage fathers to take on a bigger role in child-raising." In 2016, then Senior Minister of State Josephine Teo announced that we would legislate the second week of GPPL and increase SPL from one week to four weeks.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The enhancements were supported by Members of Parliament (MPs), such as Mr Desmond Choo, who raised in Parliament in 2016, as to whether the Government would legislate a second week of GPPL and if the Government would increase the SPL so that more leave can be taken on by fathers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Then-MP Mr Seah Kian Peng, now Speaker, had also in 2016 suggested independent leave for each parent instead of drawing leave from the mother's maternity leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Louis Ng, in 2017, urged a review of maternity leave and paternity leave, and also filed an Adjournment Motion to extend parental leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It is clear from the progressive enhancements to parental leave that the Government wants to support young parents in their caregiving needs and regularly reviews policies to push the envelope to support young parents even more.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The COVID-19 period of early 2020 to 2022 upended work structures and world economies were plunged into a period of economic uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Singapore was not spared but we were able to incorporate flexible workplace arrangements and work from home.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Young parents and working adults adjusted their working arrangements.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As we came out of COVID-19, the Government continued its strong support for families by announcing at last year's Budget policy enhancements that strengthened financial and work-life support for parents.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Baby Bonus Cash Gift was increased for all birth orders, and we enhanced the Child Development Account First Step Grant and raised Government co-matching caps for Singaporean children born on or after 14 February 2023.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Since 1 January 2024, we doubled the GPPL to four weeks, with the additional two weeks provided on a voluntary basis.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We also increased Unpaid Infant Care Leave to 12 days per parent per year in their child's first two years.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Government regularly engages young parents to see how we can support their parenthood journey.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Many parents continue to express concerns with managing family and work responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Increasingly, we see that younger generations of Singaporeans place greater emphasis on having a balance between work and personal commitments.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: They also value more family time even as they build their careers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Our social and work norms are changing, and we should, as a society, evolve to support them.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This includes working with employers to foster more family-friendly workplaces so that we can better support parents in their aspirations to do well both in work and in raising their children at the same time.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In particular, parents have shared that work-life support is especially critical during the child's first 18 months, when care needs tend to be the greatest.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Most parents prefer to personally care for their infants or tap on the help of trusted family members.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, family support is expected to decline as family sizes shrink and many grandparents work longer or prefer to spend their retirement years on other pursuits.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, we need to provide stronger caregiving support for parents in the early stages of their child's life and enable them to be more involved in caring for their infants.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This comprises 16 weeks of maternity leave, four weeks of paternity leave and 10 weeks of shared parental leave from 1 April 2026.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These enhancements are significant steps that the Government is taking to normalise paternal involvement in child-raising and provide both parents with greater support in caring for their infants together.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In addition, parents with young children are entitled to Government-Paid Childcare Leave and Extended Childcare Leave for their caregiving needs.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Those who might require more time to take care of their newborns can also utilise their Unpaid Infant Care Leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In formulating our parental leave policies, we have studied overseas experiences.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Some other countries provide longer durations of parental leave, but at varying levels of pay.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For example, in the United Kingdom (UK), parents enjoy longer maternity leave, shorter paternity leave and longer parental leave, but maternity leave and paternity leave are compensated at reduced pay and parental leave is unpaid.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Some countries, such as the United States (US), do not have paid maternity leave, paternity leave or shared parental leave at all.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For Singapore, while the combined duration of our parental leave provisions is shorter, most of it is fully paid.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: With the leave enhancements in this Bill, we will further extend the duration of paid leave that parents can take to care for their infants.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In considering Singapore's leave enhancements, we also engaged parents, consulted tripartite partners and employer representatives to ensure that we strike the right balance between parents' caregiving needs and employers' manpower and business needs.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Government worked closely with tripartite partners to design the new SPL scheme and update the conditions surrounding our parental leave provisions to better address both employees' and employers' concerns, which I will go into more detail later.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We hope that these enhancements will provide parents with more assurance as they go ahead with their plans to fulfil their family aspirations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Child Development Co-Savings (Amendment) Bill that is currently before this House seeks to give effect to the enhancements to the GPPL and SPL schemes.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We will also introduce new employment protections as well as other operational and administrative changes.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Fathers play an important role in partnering their wives in sharing the duty of raising their children.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We want to encourage shared parental responsibility and enable fathers to be more involved in child-raising.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Research also shows that greater paternal involvement in a child's early years has positive effects on the child's development and family well-being.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: With the additional two weeks of GPPL, we hope that fathers will make good use of the four weeks to care for and bond with their newborns.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Clauses 9, 11 and 12 set out the main provisions for the enhancements to the GPPL scheme.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These apply to fathers of children born on or after 1 April 2025, or with an Estimated Date of Delivery on or after 1 April 2025, as well as adoptive fathers where the eligibility date of application to adopt a child is on or after 1 April 2025.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Correspondingly, clauses 11 and 12 will double the amount of payment that an eligible employee is entitled to receive from his employer, as well as the limits for the reimbursement by the Government to an employer for that payment.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This scheme will allow parents to have more time off work to bond with and care for their infants.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We have designed this new scheme such that the additional weeks of legislated parental leave can be taken by both fathers and mothers to emphasise shared parental responsibility.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The following clauses set out the main provisions for the new SPL scheme, and the new Shared Parental Leave Benefit scheme for working parents of a Singapore Citizen child born or with an estimated date of delivery on or after 1 April 2025.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Clause 6 will entitle working parents who are eligible for Government-Paid Maternity Leave (GPML), paternity leave and adoption leave under the Act, to the new SPL, and sets out the requirements for a valid sharing arrangement for the new SPL between two parents.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The allocation can be varied according to clause 23 to provide parents with the flexibility to use the leave in a way that meets their caregiving needs.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This flexibility has to be balanced against the employers' need for some certainty of the employees' intended absences so they can plan for covering arrangements to ensure business continuity.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The same clause, therefore, also provides that parents who wish to change their sharing arrangement on their own may do so within the first four weeks after their child's birth or, for an adopted child, within the first four weeks after the eligibility date of application to adopt.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Thereafter, employees must obtain their employer's agreement before further changes can be made.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Clause 6 will also allow employees and employers to mutually agree on how the new SPL will be taken, as long as it is taken within 12 months of the child's birth.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We understand that some parents may wish to have the flexibility to take this leave over a longer period.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, we have to balance this against the challenges that employers may face in their manpower planning if the leave-taking period stretches beyond one year.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In the absence of a mutual agreement, employees are entitled to take their allocated share of the new SPL in a continuous block within the first 26 weeks of the child's birth, with sufficient notice given to their employer.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I will share more about the notice period required further in my speech.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Similarly, clause 6 will entitle working parents who are eligible for GPML, GPPL and Government-Paid Adoption Benefits to the new Shared Parental Benefits scheme.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: These cash benefit-equivalent schemes are intended for working parents who do not qualify for leave due to their employment arrangements such as employees on short-term contracts, or contracts that expire before the child’s birth.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Employers can then use the wage savings to hire temporary workers or make other operational adjustments when their employee is away on parental leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As the new SPL scheme is meant to replace the existing SPL scheme, clause 8 will amend the eligibility criteria for the existing SPL scheme such that it will no longer apply for a Singapore Citizen child born or with an Estimated Date of Delivery on or after 1 April 2025.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This brings me to the third aspect of this Bill, new notice period requirements and employment protections, which seek to balance the needs of employers and employees utilising the parental leave schemes.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: With the longer duration of leave, employers will need sufficient lead time to make covering arrangements when their employees are away.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Employees must inform employers at least four weeks before commencing continuous GPML, GPPL, adoption leave and the new SPL.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This will give employers lead time to plan for covering arrangements and make operational adjustments.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: While this is the legislated minimum requirement, I urge employees to exercise responsibility when taking the leave, to provide notice as early as possible and work through covering arrangements with your peers and employers before you go on leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We will update employment protections to give parents peace of mind when they go on parental leave entitlements.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Today, it is unlawful for an employer to dismiss or give a notice of dismissal to a female employee when she is on maternity leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Employers who do so today will be guilty of an offence and be liable on conviction to a fine or imprisonment, or both.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This means it will be unlawful for an employer to dismiss or give a notice of dismissal to employees on GPPL or adoption leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For the case of the new SPL, we want to strike a balance between providing both parents with a longer period of leave to care for their child in the first year, while allowing employers to carry out fair employment decisions during this extended period of leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Hence, parents on SPL will not receive the same protection as those on GPML, GPPL and adoption leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, employees who consider themselves to be wrongfully dismissed when taking this leave, may seek recourse under the Employment Act.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The upcoming Workplace Fairness Legislation will also strengthen protections against workplace discrimination.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I hope that these new protections will give our parents, including fathers, more assurance to take their maternity, paternity and adoption leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Beyond legislation, I urge employers to show your support for the employees taking parental leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For instance, by putting in place fair appraisal systems that recognise their contributions and not penalise employees simply for having taken parental leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Managers and colleagues can also help to build a more family-friendly culture by being understanding of colleagues who need to take leave to care for their children.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: On the part of parents, I also encourage you to reciprocate when colleagues need to take time off to tend to their personal needs.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The other amendments pertain to clauses to improve operational efficiency and clarity.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Clause 16 of the Bill will clarify that the limits for reimbursement of an employer will be implemented on a “per parent” basis for a parent with multiple employers, or a parent who is both employed and self-employed.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For example, an employee’s payment from a single employer is capped at $2,500 per week and the single employer’s reimbursement from the Government is similarly capped at $2,500 per week.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This ensures parity on the amount of Government-paid leave granted to all parents, regardless of the number of employments that they have.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This amendment is also one of the Ministry of Social and Family Development's (MSF’s) corrective actions to address the Auditor-General's Office's (AGO’s) observations of possible irregularities in the payment of Government-Paid Leave Schemes in July this year.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Clause 16 of the Bill will determine that the sequence of leave taking under the Act such that employees are deemed to be consuming their entitlement to GPML, GPPL or adoption leave in full first, before consuming their entitlement for SPL.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This is in line with our intent that all employees should consume their GPML, GPPL or adoption leave before commencing the new SPL.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It is a joyful but also demanding period for the couple who needs to tend to the high care needs of their infant.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We hope the leave enhancements covered in this Bill will give working parents greater peace of mind to focus on caring for their child during their early years.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We will also continue to enhance other caregiving options to provide more support to parents.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, this role of supporting parents in their parenthood journey cannot be played by the Government alone.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Employers, for instance, have to be supportive of their employees, especially fathers, going on parental leave and should implement family-friendly workplaces.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This will help employees returning to work post-leave can manage their work and parenting responsibilities well.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: (In Mandarin):   Family is the bedrock of our society.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We hope that parents and children can build good relationships so that we have stronger foundation for our families.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Many parents have told us that it is very challenging for them to balance both work and family commitments, especially when their children are in the infancy stage.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I urge more employers, businesses and community partners, to work with us to build a Singapore Made For Families.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This reflects a broad societal trend that young Singaporeans want better familial support, before they commit to having children.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am glad that the Government has, in response, made big moves to foster a more family-friendly Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I also welcome the new Shared Parental Benefits, a cash benefit-equivalent scheme for parents who are not eligible for the SPL due to their employment arrangements.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This would ensure parity for those who work as short-term contract workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While the changes will help to create a more family-friendly Singapore and encourage more couples to have more babies, one segment of couples have felt left out, as the changes will only take effect from 1 April 2025.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am referring to, of course, couples who are already expecting, with their estimated delivery dates sometime between 1 January and 31 March 2025.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I understand that Government schemes must start from a certain date and that there will inevitably be some that will be left out as a result.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This would mirror the additional two weeks of GPPL for fathers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am sure that couples with children born in the first quarter of 2025 would deeply appreciate this.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This reflects the broader trend of fractional work, where an employee works for multiple employers, but on a shorter schedule.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am therefore happy that the Ministry is clarifying the Act to ensure that the total amount of reimbursements to employers of a working parent with multiple employments would be the same as the total amount of reimbursements made to the employer of a working parent with a single employment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, having multiple employers will result in greater complexities and potential disputes in the event that one employer finds themselves paying more than others.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Having clear guidelines will reduce potential disputes and protect our fractional workers from being discriminated against, due to their pregnancy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I also commonly hear from my grassroots volunteers that they sometimes utilised much of their annual leave to care for their young children who have fallen ill.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Some even had to take unpaid leave, if their child has lower immunity.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Government currently provides up to six days of Government-Paid Childcare Leave for parents who have children below seven years old and two days of Extended Childcare Leave for those with primary school-going children.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to parents that I have spoken to, this is inadequate and they hope that more support can be given in terms of childcare leave.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Could the Government consider staggering the number of Government-Paid Childcare Leave?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For instance, more paid leave days could be provided to parents when the child is in infant care and nursery, and this tapers off gradually as the child enters kindergarten and primary school.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Having more paid childcare leave when the child is youngest and requires the most care, will certainly go a long way in helping parents cope with the inevitable healthcare challenges in their children’s early years.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As we enhance marriage and parenthood benefits and continue to provide hefty Government subsidies for preschools, we can do more to alleviate any anxieties that might serve as an impediment to prospective parents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, maternity insurance is not compulsory and insurers are allowed to reject applicants with pre-existing health conditions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Under such a scheme, we can sufficiently risk-pool and mothers with pre-existing health conditions will therefore not be denied coverage.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In closing, I would like to commend the Government for continuing to make bold and decisive moves to enhance both marriage and parenthood benefits.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am confident that these measures will help make Singapore more family-friendly and hopefully encourage more couples to have children.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that the Government will continue to evolve the scheme and also consider my suggestions to help young parents better cope in the early childhood years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The SPL scheme was also introduced on top of the GPPL and GPML enhancements.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With Singapore's TFR dropping to a record low of 0.97 in 2023, such measures are certainly a step forward in promoting parenthood amongst couples.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In my speech today, I will share my thoughts on several of these measures and other points which I believe, are important to consider including paternity leave, SPL, flexible work arrangements (FWAs) and childcare leave provisions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: During the debate on the Women's Development White Paper in 2022, I highlighted how policy moves such as increasing one's GPPL entitlement would encourage more fathers to take a more active role in their parenting and household responsibilities, and thus help nurture gender equality within society by shunning traditional gender norms.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In Singapore, however, it is deeply concerning that just over half of fathers even took paternity leave to begin with.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As someone who had taken my full share of two weeks of paternity leave twice, I find it hard to understand, especially when it is an all-hands-on-deck situation at home immediately following a newborn's birth.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In my speech on the Budget 2023 debate, I shared that while the move to raise GPPL from two weeks to four weeks is no doubt welcome, I noted that this was purely on the voluntary basis on the part of employers and wondered if the then-Deputy Prime Minister's message that we want paternal involvement to be the norm in our society could in practice turn out as being construed as paternal involvement is voluntary.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The move to make the four weeks of paternity leave mandatory is thus a welcome change.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: That said, given our utilisation of paternity leave today, where only just over half of fathers take paternity leave and the median paternity leave taken by eligible fathers is only just over a week, I wonder if would-be fathers would be in a position to take the full entitlement of the expanded paternity leave and, importantly, feel comfortable doing so.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps it is worth considering having the Government payment of paternity leave to employers to be contingent on the utilisation of at least half of the full four weeks, at two weeks of paternity leave, before gradually increasing these over time.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This could further entrench the notion that paternal involvement is important and necessary, while taking into account employers' concerns.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is certainly a welcome move which I wholeheartedly agree with.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As part of the Workers' Party (WP) manifesto in 2020, we proposed a shared parental leave scheme that entitles parents to 24 weeks of Government-paid leave to be shared between mothers and fathers as they choose, with a minimum of 12 weeks to be granted to the mother and four weeks to the father.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This was a point which I have also reiterated during the debate on the Empowering Women Motion in August 2021 and the Women's Development White Paper in 2022, as have my other WP colleagues.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As my Sengkang team mate Ms He Ting Ru described in her speech in October 2020, the current Government policy back then, which allows fathers to share only up to four weeks of the mother's leave, reinforces the outdated notion that childcare is primarily the mother's responsibility rather than promoting equal parenting roles.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: That being said, while the default position is that each parent is allocated half of the SPL to encourage shared parental responsibility, I wonder if this is likely to be the case in reality.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I acknowledge that we need to give parents the ability to decide what is best for their own families, but part of the requirements of the new SPL is that changes to the leave-sharing arrangements should be made within four weeks after the child's birth.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Any changes thereafter will require mutual agreement between parents and their employers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Likewise, I agree that we need to acknowledge the potential impact on business operations as a result of employees' parental leave arrangements.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But can we consider putting in place mechanisms to better facilitate or mediate issues faced by parents when making changes to SPL arrangements, especially when the needs of either parent's employers may not be aligned?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, while parents may have decided on an equal sharing of SPL, the mother's employer may have a new and time-sensitive work project that comes up and the father's employer may not see it in their own business interests to agree to the extension of the parental leave.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If this is not possible, can we consider extending the eligibility period for the parental leave to be taken within 24 months of the child's date of birth, instead of within 12 months from the child's birth?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Doing so can also give both employers and parents the flexibility they need to respond to changing circumstances and needs within the households and also at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This brings me to my point on FWAs, which I have spoken about on numerous occasions in this House.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Crucially, it stops short of legislating the right to request for FWAs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, the recent uptick in employers such as Grab and Amazon requiring all employees to return to office for all five days of the week have undone the progress made to normalise FWAs in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: FWAs are also important in the context of our current childcare leave provisions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we cannot legislate for FWAs, can we then at least ensure that parents are able to care for the needs of their child via increasing the number of days of childcare leave, or to have it on a per-child basis?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As many parents with young children may know, they will need to take significant time off from work to care for their children as they often tend to fall ill.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For instance, I have shared in my Adjournment Motion speech on FWAs in 2023 that I had clocked 20 visits to a paediatrician over a period of nine months.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With medical leave durations ranging from three days to about five days, how can parents cope without additional childcare leave or FWAs?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In response to calls by Members of this House to enhance childcare leave provisions, the Government has articulated its concern about the impact that increasing such leave benefits have on the manpower and operational needs of their businesses.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, seeing how we are facing a TFR crisis of our generation, perhaps the Government should channel greater efforts towards granting Singaporeans who wish to start a family the opportunity to achieve that dream.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Further, employers could still stand to benefit as it has the effect of boosting staff retention and productivity.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Nonetheless, should increasing the statutory childcare leave entitlements by a couple of days be deemed as having a substantial adverse effect on businesses, FWAs that parents can actually have could present itself as a viable solution.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Given that my first child was born in September 2019 and less than a year later, I was elected together with my Sengkang team mates in July 2020.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A year later, in November 2021, my second child was born and his birthday is in a couple of weeks.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Like many of my peers with young children, to say that parenthood is like a roller coaster ride is not an understatement.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With many ups and downs, unexpected twists and turns, where you could be screaming in terror one moment and crying tears of joy in the other.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I have absolutely no regrets being a father, but I also feel deeply the sacrifices and difficulties that a working parent has to go through in the Singapore that we live in today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For some of my peers who have decided not to have children, I do not blame them at all when they question whether or not all the sacrifices that are necessary in being a parent is actually worth their time, money and effort.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Why wake up at 3.00 am in the morning for a feed when you could be sleeping in over the weekend and then have brunch?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Why fret over paying for diapers, food, childcare, clothing when you could be on a nice ski holiday to Japan?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Why scramble to pick up your kids from school when you could be striving to advance your career in the office?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As lawmakers, we cannot force Singaporeans to have more children, just as how we cannot force Members of this House to lead by example and meet the replacement TFR of 2.1.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Just so that we can place the sustainability of Singapore as a nation as an utmost priority.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This Bill, if passed, is a significant signal to our young Singaporeans that the Government will make significant policy moves to support their family journeys.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many young couples desire to be highly involved parents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Besides resources and housing, many of them worry if they would have the time and space to care for their children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They want to give the best to their children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are many needs, and there are already many policy interventions that are necessary and some of them are already in place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The first year of birth is often the most challenging.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As with all parents, we all struggle with caring for our babies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is nearly always all hands on deck or crib in that first year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I remember speaking about this issue in 2016, a few months after the birth of my first child.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The weariness and eye bags were very evident then.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Further supporting young Singaporeans in the first year of birth is indeed the right move.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But this Bill also sends a strong message that there needs to be a greater and faster evolution in gender-based family stereotypes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our women and mothers bear a greater responsibility at home.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While we have made progress over the years, it is true that our women and mothers bear the lion's share of the burden.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The differences between the male and female labour force participation rates are evident, so our mothers will need greater caregiving support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But we also need a strong societal signal that everyone can play a role to narrow the gender gap, especially those born out of cultural norms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It also encourages fathers to play a greater role in parenting.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With smaller family sizes, young couples are increasingly finding it difficult to manage both their aspirations with their family commitments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Most of us will have heard of young couples shelving their plans to start families because of the lack of caregiving support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe that the enhanced leave structure will go a long way in helping couples who wish to start or expand their families better manage their responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The legislative signal can promote an important signal to employers and peers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But there are also larger societal shifts that will be imperative to the success of this policy shift and, in fact, the SPL.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Bill places a renewed emphasis on the roles that fathers can have on parenting.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is a cultural norm, perhaps more so in Asian societies, that caregiving is still seen as that falling within the domain of mothers, while fathers are the traditional breadwinner.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe that such cultural norms are already changing, especially amongst our younger Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But such outdated notions remain in Singapore society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The enhanced GPPL, whilst a shift in policy, cannot, by itself, drive this cultural change.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For that shift to happen, we need both fathers and mothers to contribute within the home and in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is why I would like to call on fathers to utilise the GPPL to take on an active, meaningful role in raising their children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Research has shown that fathers who actively participate in caregiving for their children build stronger bonds with their children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Downstream effects of undertaking such an active role include positive cognitive and social developmental outcomes in children and can include positive labour-market outcomes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Even while our young couples play their role in stepping up to their family commitments, supportive workplaces are key to making this aspiration a reality.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some single or older workers might be asked to cover duties for their child-bearing colleagues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some employers have lamented where would the additional manpower come from.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These are valid concerns, but the low birth rate is a national collective issue.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I encourage companies to support our workers who would need to cover duties either with incentives or to hire additional manpower from the Government payment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Workplaces play a crucial role in creating a positive environment that supports the Government's family-friendly policies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There will, indeed, be sacrifices from all quarters, but we had also made it work back then in the earlier years, where there were significantly more births.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Besides, without a supportive environment, some women, or in fact men, might decide to leave the company.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, it is a good human capital practice to retain talent in the company by providing support to our young parents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Legislatively, the Bill does much to ensure that fathers enjoy the benefits and protection arising from GPPL.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, the proposed amendments to section 12H of the Bill introduces protection for an employee against dismissals during the period that such an employee is taking the GPPL.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I also note and support that the same protections are also now extended to parents on adoption leave.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe that by doing so, we will send a stronger signal towards the Government's stance on such dismissals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, whilst such protection does provide some comfort to employees, some workers, especially fathers, may still hesitate to fully utilise their entitlement due to workplace cultures that might frown upon long absences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is where inclusive workplace cultures become paramount.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: From a business standpoint, the concerns of employers are real.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I do acknowledge that our small and medium enterprises (SMEs) may face operational constraints in complying with the new legislation, and I would like to urge the Ministry to consider the constraints faced by these SMEs and help them to adopt inclusive workplaces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement stands ready to assist the Ministry on this front.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I have spoken on various occasions on the importance of closing the gender pay gap in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The gender pay gap has been attributed to the fact that women shoulder a disproportionate burden of caregiving responsibilities which, in turn, causes them, or might cause them, to fall behind in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The time away from work can cause our women to lose out on work and wage progression.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While we have made significant progress in the past decade to narrow our gender pay gap, more must be done.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In turn, we can change the outdated notions of the roles of men and women within family and level the playing field between genders in the long run.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is worth noting that this Bill will likely provide a positive, long-term effect on the next generation of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I am hopeful that children who grow up seeing both parents share caregiving responsibilities will thereafter carry these norms into their own lives when they start their own families in the future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is a call to action for us all.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For fathers, it is an invitation to play larger roles in parenting.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For workplaces, it is a call for stakeholders to cultivate a supportive environment that is understanding of the dual responsibilities of both mothers and fathers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For society, Singapore at large, it is a reminder that gender equality is not just an issue women should care about, but instead, a social imperative for our society to flourish.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These changes had been announced during the National Day Rally.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Although more parental leave alone might not necessarily have an immediate significant effect on our TFR, we believe it will create a positive effect as it gives potential parents peace of mind to take time off work to build secure and strong relationships with their newborn children, setting an important foundation for the long journey ahead.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We support the amendments to increase mandatory paid paternity leave and introduce protection for fathers against a notice of dismissal during paid paternity leave, which is similar to the current protection mothers have during paid maternity leave.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These amendments send an important message that both parents are co-partners in a marriage and in starting a new family, and provide the crucial opportunity for both parents to be physically present to take on child-minding responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Research has uncovered evidence pointing to the crucial role played by fathers in affecting not just newborn health and the subsequent development of a child, but also maternal health, postpartum and beyond.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A father who is involved from the very start in the caring of a child provides important support to the mother, especially during the immediate postpartum period when mothers face the risk of postpartum depression.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A mother who is both mentally and physically healthy is, in turn, better able to provide optimum care for the child.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Indeed, a longitudinal study conducted in Singapore found that fathers who were involved in their infant's birth were more actively involved in infant care at six months postpartum, highlighting how active participation from the start carries forward to the later periods in the child's life.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fathers also play a unique and critical role in the different stages of childhood development, affecting the socio-emotional and cognitive development of their children.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is, therefore, heartening to see that the Government is implementing policy changes to help fathers fulfil their important role in parenting.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Besides the duration of paid parental leave, we believe that there are many other factors at play which affect the ability and willingness of Singaporeans to have children.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In our view, these other factors include the cost of living, especially the cost of housing, healthcare and education, as well as employment policies that have an impact on job security, the rates of unemployment and underemployment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this regard, PSP strongly supports the introduction through this Bill of protection for fathers against a notice of dismissal during paid paternity leave, which is similar to the current provisions for mothers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As our cost of living continues to rise, job security is ever more important, especially to a couple who are contemplating on starting a new family and having children.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In totality, moving towards more parental leave and the gradual equalisation of maternity and paternity leave are both beneficial to building stronger marriages and families, and PSP appreciates the Government's efforts thus far to work with tripartite partners to establish the norms of fathers taking leave to care for and bond with their infants.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also believe that it is important for the Government to address the high cost of living in Singapore and consider employer incentives to create a more conducive work culture, as these also affect the ability and willingness of Singaporeans to start a family and have children.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Research has shown that fathers not only have a significant impact on the health of newborns and subsequent child development but are also important to the mothers' postpartum health.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP therefore supports the Government's implementation of these policy changes to support fathers in playing their crucial role in the parenting process.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The issue of low fertility rates has troubled our country for many years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP believes that, in addition to the duration of paid parental leave, there are many factors affecting the ability and willingness of our citizens to have children.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, PSP supports the Bill.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The move towards a default 50-50 split on shared parental leave between parents is a bold step in the right direction.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This structure sends a strong message about the normalisation of shared caregiving between women and men, not just at home, but also in the workplace and in society at large.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With this flexibility, fathers are empowered and equipped to step up, take on more active roles at home, building stronger relationships with their children, strengthening marital bonds and setting a positive example to our children.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond this, by being invested in the everyday runnings of the household, fathers also empower mothers to return to the workplace with peace of mind.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Caregiving responsibilities and, believe it or not, housework are common reasons given for this.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A 2021 Ipsos and United Women Singapore survey also found that while close to nine in 10 Singaporeans agree that household chores can be equally shared by husband and wife, gender-defined roles still exist in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The same study found that, in reality, more women take on the daily responsibilities of cleaning and laundry, tasks that take up daily attention, while men contribute by taking on household repairs and management of technological devices.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, Mr Speaker, would we not agree that many working mothers, especially those returning to their careers, would benefit immensely from the support of a partner who is actively involved in household responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the enhancements to the paternity and shared parental leave schemes, we hope to see more fathers encouraged to lean in and support their partners beyond traditional expectations.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, in order for this to happen, workplace norms would need to evolve to not only support, but encourage more fathers to take up these leave schemes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As part of change management, companies must have open communications between management and employees, institute fair outcomes-based performance appraisals and create positive role models.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Initiatives, such as townhalls, lunchtime parenting talks and even mentorship circles, are good ways to spark discussion within the workplace and I would like to ask our Ministry if support and resources can be availed to companies in their change culture process.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the passing of our recent Platform Workers Bill, our platform workers are recognised for being employee-like and the Labour Movement thanks the Government for taking in our recommendation to include platform operators' Central Provident Fund (CPF) contributions in the calculation of Government-paid leave payments.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This adjustment ensures parity with salaried employees and recognising CPF contributions in leave calculations reinforces the idea that all workers deserve fair treatment when it comes to their parental leave entitlements.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While these enhancements address the critical first set of adjustments families must take after their child's birth, FWAs, enhanced caregiving leave, extended family support and a trusted ecosystem of care providers must be in place to support our families.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In part, this is because, this is not about a one-size-fits-all FWA, but one that revolves around requests.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, revolving itself around the work hours and the work plans of our caregivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Paid caregiving leave was second, at 64% and this was a good 20% lower than FWAs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some of our workers have shared their apprehension when it comes to asking for FWAs, citing that they may face backlash or future discrimination from their employers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In equipping workers and employers with the upcoming rollout, the Labour Movement and the Tripartite Workgroup for Flexible Work Arrangement Requests has provided resources, such as templated employee handbooks, training for workers, case studies for companies.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe the upcoming Workplace Fairness Legislation will also, no doubt, set additional protective safety nets.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But how can MSF further support our parents and caregivers by helping to normalise FWAs in the workplace?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can the popular Becky the Bunny "Families For Life" theme become an expanded campaign in workplaces to spark frank discussions and family-friendly programmes in the workplace?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This could include encouraging companies to adopt progressive leave practices, such as allowing singles to take childcare leave to help look after their nieces and nephews.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With these enhancements, we are moving closer to a society where every parent, regardless of gender, is empowered and equipped to contribute meaningfully to their family, workplace and community.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is a very forward-looking policy change that demonstrates our commitment to strong family values and a supportive society.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Freelancers make up about one in ten of Singapore's resident workforce.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They welcome the Bill and look forward to the enhancements.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, some have raised concerns on how the Bill would be received by service buyers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Before I proceed, I declare my role as Director for NTUC's Freelancer and Self-Employed Unit.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: However, some freelancers have found the journey of becoming a mother distressing.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, some freelance instructors shared about abrupt termination of their contracts after disclosing their pregnancy status to clients.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Being dumped by clients in such manner is hurtful and runs counter to this Bill's push for progressive, family-friendly policies.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: My Parliamentary Question at the recent 14 October 2024 Sitting, thus sought to know if MOM would extend maternity protection to Singaporeans engaged in non-standard forms of employment should the contracts of these freelancers, such as dependent contractors, be terminated on grounds related to pregnancy.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, would MSF consider working with MOM and Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP), to state upfront, in the Tripartite Standard on contracting with self-employed persons, that a service buyer should consider substitution options than to terminate the contract of a freelancer who must absent herself due to pregnancy and/or childbirth?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Could I also seek assurance from the Government that should a freelancer approach TAFEP and/or the Small Claims Tribunal about losing a contract or contracted gig after disclosing her pregnancy status to the client, the authorities would not condone such pregnancy discrimination?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to seek clarification on the amendment where workers with multiple employment arrangements would be reimbursed on a per-parent basis instead of per-employment basis.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: How would this amendment be implemented for persons who are both employees and self-employed?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications sought, I support the Bill and look forward to this decisive step towards a fair and inclusive work environment for freelancers and employees.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have spoken up many times in this House about providing more paternity leave and equalising paternity leave, for making our policies fairer and sending a strong message that looking after a child is not just a mother's duty, but also that of the father's.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill will give our parents the most precious thing of all, more time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My parenthood journey with my daughters Ella, Katie and Poppy is the most rewarding journey I have taken.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This journey started with paternity leave that allowed me to spend precious time with my babies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope many more fathers will be able to experience the same.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As my colleagues know, I am a housefly when it comes to asking for more.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even as Minister Indranee swats and shoos me, I keep coming back for more.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, even as we celebrate this huge step forward, I also hope that we can look into three further points.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on how we can encourage fathers to take more paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government has sent a strong signal to employers and fathers by increasing mandatory paternity leave to four weeks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This legislative signal will have to be accompanied by softer measures to encourage and inspire fathers to actually take the leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I believe that fathers do want to spend more time with their newborn child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many fathers I speak to tell me they do not have a supportive environment at their workplace and so, they do not feel they can take the leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Taking the full four weeks of GPPL does not mean fathers can become their infant's main caregivers, but it means they can be more present in the first few weeks of their infant's life – precious and important few weeks – and start their fatherhood journey on a strong footing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the Committee of Supply of 2022, Minister Indranee shared her thoughts on paternity leave, I quote, "We see more fathers wanting to be involved.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Which is why, both at the Committee of Supply and now, I am reiterating, as, indeed, Mr Ng is, that it is actually better for your organisation if you are family-friendly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is better for your organisation if you support fathers to take paternity leave and, of course, mothers as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is something that we need to work with the Tripartite Partners on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Ng can be reassured that this is an area of work we will continue to look at." Unquote.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad the Minister has provided the reassurances and, indeed, steps have been taken, but it is timely to receive another reassurance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State and Minister Indranee share what steps the Ministry will be taking to encourage fathers to take more paternity leave?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on helping low-income fathers to take their paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A longitudinal study by the National University of Singapore Prof Jean Yeung found that fathers in more labour-intensive or lower-income roles are less likely to take paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She said that this segment of the population and their employers should be a key focus for policymakers and paternity leave policy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To quote Prof Yeung, "They may fear they will lose their jobs if they take the leave, so that they feel some pressure from their bosses and co-workers for taking this leave." Being a new father is stressful.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They have to care and provide for a new life.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For lower-income fathers in precarious jobs, the stress is even more acute.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fathers should not have to choose between spending time with their babies and keeping their jobs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have laws which generally provide against unfair dismissal, but these may not provide sufficient assurance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State share how we can have more targeted support for lower-income fathers to take their paternity leave?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final point is on equalising parental leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad that the default position is that the 10 weeks of shared parental leave will be equally shared.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, maternity leave is still four times that of paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The big gap between maternity and paternity leave entrenches gender stereotypes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A 2019 Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) research paper stated that “family policies in Singapore continue to signal that childcare is a woman’s responsibility and reinforces gender stereotypes”.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Because we give fathers less leave, they do not get to develop the skills and confidence needed to care for their kids.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Thus, this, the IPS study finds, causes them to leave childcare to mothers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: More recently, a Cultivate SG-commissioned poll done in mid-2024 on parenthood and work found that material and financial provision is the most common perceived role for fathers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In contrast, mothers are associated with care-oriented roles.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that we will eventually equalise the amount of paternity and maternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is an ambitious call but there are concrete steps we can take now.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us start by setting a target year, perhaps 2030, or later, for equalising paternity and maternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can increase paternity leave in phases, like we are doing now, and give our employers time to plan ahead, while also providing a clear signal of our intentions to reduce gender perceptions of parenthood.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A baby will only remain a baby for a very short time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They will grow up before we even realise it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The thing about life is, we cannot rewind time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, my advice to young parents here is, your children need you, they need you desperately and they need you only for a very, very transient time in their lives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our policies are changing and we are heading in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill goes beyond a routine policy update.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It reflects our commitment to supporting the well-being of families which, in turn, strengthens both our economy and society.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As a father to three kids, my youngest just two years and four months old, and a business owner, I fully appreciate the priority of family.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Whether it is attending to a sick child or ensuring they are receiving vaccinations, family will and should always come first.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is a value that the business community understands and respects, as we all recognise that a strong family foundation ultimately supports a stable and productive workforce.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, I do have a few clarifications on the SPL scheme.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: First, section 12DA provides a solid framework, but we can do more to encourage companies to be progressive in supporting parents.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill states that if a newly hired employee meets all requirements but has not yet completed three months of employment, and the employer grants them SPL, the Government may reimburse the employer.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Second, for parents with multiple jobs or a combination of employment and self-employment, section 12M provides much-needed support.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, clear guidance on managing claims and reimbursement limits would alleviate potential concerns, particularly for employers.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Employers may, in good faith, pay out the full leave benefits to employees but could later find that Government reimbursements are less than expected.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This could increase administrative complexity and even require employers to claw back amounts from these part-time employees – an uncomfortable situation for all involved.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Clarification from the Government on how these cases will be handled would be invaluable in reducing these risks for employers and ensuring smooth implementation of these provisions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Third, the Bill also introduces penalties for employers who "without reasonable cause" fail to grant SPL.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: While employees have the flexibility to take leave within 12 months, certain situations may arise where immediate leave requests pose significant challenges.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, if a small business with limited staff cannot immediately accommodate leave without major disruptions, would that constitute a reasonable cause for delay, especially if the employee insists on taking it at that time?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For sectors with critical peak seasons, such as retail during holidays, could an employer reasonably defer leave if an employee insists on taking it during such high demand times?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The business community supports these initiatives as essential for workforce sustainability and economic resilience.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, the extension of SPL presents operational challenges, especially for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Smaller businesses with lean teams must manage workload distribution, find temporary staffing and plan for the re-integration of employees returning from leave.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For highly specialised roles, finding a suitable temporary replacement is not always straightforward.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Re-integrating employees after extended leave also requires careful planning to maintain productivity.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs often incur additional costs during overlapping periods when both returning employees and temporary staff are needed.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We all understand that time away to care for a sick child or to meet other family needs is essential and should be respected fully.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, fostering a supportive work environment is a shared responsibility.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I encourage employees to give ample notice whenever possible in planning their parental leave and using this time with the purpose it is intended for, dedicating it to family.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: When everyone respects these principles, it strengthens trust between employers and employees and creates a smoother experience for all involved.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I also urge employees, when possible, to remain flexible and reachable for urgent matters during their leave.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, if you are in charge of IT in your organisation and it is hit by a serious virus, such as cloudstrike, and your colleagues need your help, please be there for them.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This sense of mutual assistance reinforces trust, promotes teamwork and nurtures a workplace culture that benefits everyone.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, it is essential that both employers and employees acknowledge the efforts of colleagues who take on additional responsibilities during someone’s parental leave.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Recognising and appreciating their contributions go a long way in fostering respect and a spirit of collaboration that supports the entire organisation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: By setting a new standard in progressive workplace policies, we enhance our global competitiveness and quality of life for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding my questions, I support this Bill wholeheartedly.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The provisions in these latest amendments to the CDCA Bill represent a significant step towards realising a vision of society where healthy equal parenting is the norm, where dads get to be a much bigger part of their children’s lives from those vital early months, and moms get to continue to pursue their careers with the support of their partners.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But I want to stress a key point.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Realising this vision is not just about the personal choices of individual moms and dads.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Realising this vision requires a systemic cultural shift, where attitudes within workplaces and society at large are supportive of families, and those who take parental leave are not made to feel guilty or regret for doing so.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have heard the concerns of employers over the operational challenges, as well as from colleagues, especially singles or childless colleagues, who worry that that they will be forced to pick up the slack for colleagues on parental leave with nothing in return for them.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I do not trivialise these points of view.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But I believe the importance of providing more support to families means we must go beyond these concerns.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: First, we must ensure that men and women who take the parental leave that they are entitled to are not discriminated against.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: According to the Association of Women for Action and Research's (AWARE’s) Workplace Harassment and Discrimination Advisory, maternity discrimination from untoward job interview questions to wrongful dismissals, denials of bonuses and outright harassment is by far the most common form of discrimination seen.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But it is not just an issue for women.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Studies have also suggested that some men also fear losing their jobs if they take their paternity leave and feel pressure from their bosses and co-workers when they want to do so.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is important that the progressive moves in this Bill do not lead to unintended negative consequences.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In India in 2017, mandated paid maternity leave was increased from 12 weeks to 26 weeks.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This was attributed to a rise in firms’ reservations for hiring women in the high fertility age group, since employers alone financed the leave.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Second, we must promote a workplace culture that supports families and greater opportunities for women.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This starts with inclusive leadership and line managers who walk the talk and must be supported by moves to embed gender balanced leadership and diversity within teams, and to enhance parental support in order to help sustain the change.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Parental support here refers to not only parental leave but other forms of support before, during and after pregnancy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, progressive employers offer flexibility for medical appointments pre-delivery, FWAs post-delivery and after parental leave, and re-integration support post parental leave and childcare leave.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Line managers have an outsized impact on how any policy lands for their workers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They need to be socialised and trained on the benefits of parental leave to the company, including on recruitment and retention and to society as a whole.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In a tight labour market, such as we are in now, companies need to put their best foot forward, and the sooner they move to a supportive workplace culture, the better.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It makes a big difference when managers encourage and are role models themselves for taking up parental leave options or FWAs, so that any employee looking to do so will not feel like he or she sticks out as an exception to the norm.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is critically important that men take the new shared parental leave.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: By creating a new shared parental leave that is shared equally by mom and dad by default, versus sacrificing part of the mother's maternity leave as is the case today, which may explain the low take-up, is a great move.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If the vast majority of shared parental leave is still taken by the moms, women will continue to struggle in the workforce and women of childbearing age could be discriminated against, whether or not they want to have children.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, take-up of SPL by fathers is something we really need to track.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some organisations, especially SMEs, will need support in making the transition to this new culture.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But the fact is, there are SMEs that are doing this today, who are progressive and more should take the same step.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As for single or childless workers who fear that all these might unfairly create additional burden to them, it is important to recognise that the responsibility for arranging parental leave cover does not like with these co-workers, it is the responsibility of the employer.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Employees who take on a significantly heavier load to cover for a co-worker should be adequately compensated, or the company can look into taking on a temp worker to take over all or some of the duties.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The longer the duration of parental leave also makes me more feasible to take on temp workers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: While employees are entitled to take their parental leave, proactiveness on their part to not only give sufficient notice as required under the new provisions and to also find practical solutions to their time off and hand over work responsibility, will no doubt be appreciated.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And may I ask for a clarification from the Minister of State.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Because caring for children does not stop after 12 months.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We need to support parents to navigate caring from their children throughout their childcare years.
