speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But I feel passionately that moms and dads should have a genuine choice about how they manage parenting and work in the early years of their children's lives.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is good for dads, moms, our children, society and the economy in the long run.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Let us build a Singapore that is pro-business, pro-worker and pro-family.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The amendments proposed in this Bill demonstrate our Government's unceasing effort to make Singapore an even more conducive environment for Singaporeans to start families.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These amendments follow the slew of past measures such as enhancements to parental leave, increasing childcare availability and affordability, as well as providing more financial assistance to large families.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is an alarming sign and an existential threat to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Prospective parents would have their respectively varying concerns and reasons militating against starting a family.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Everybody's circumstances and challenges are unique and there is no silver bullet to miraculously improve Singapore's TFR overnight.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That said, I have every firm believe that our PAP Government will never stop doing its best for Singaporeans, and today, we have this Bill to improve the conditions for prospective parents, which is a step in the right direction in an endless journey.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During the recent focus group discussions organised by the PAP's Women's Wing and Friendzone, I got to listen to approximately 100 youths aged between 20 and 40 years old.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When asked whether they intend to have children, many of them candidly shared their concerns with me, that child raising comes with significant burdens – both emotionally and financially.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Amongst other comments, some of these youths painted a daunting picture with their words when they said, "marriage is hard, raising children is even harder" and "if I want to have a kid, I must be confident that I can provide him/her with the best, if I think I can't do that, I would rather not have one." As I told them at the discussion, and I repeat now, we hear you.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These are genuine concerns on at least two levels – in actuality and by perception.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Either level could be sufficient to dissuade a couple from starting a family.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The actual and/or perceived high costs of education, transportation, medical care, clothing and food, may generally cause couples to feel anxious and face challenges in sustaining their childless lifestyle, which may become or feel insurmountable should they have a child or children.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Child Development Account or in short, CDA, is a Government initiative designed to support parents in managing the costs associated with raising children.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Over the years, the Government has broadened the scope of approved uses of the CDA to cover beyond education and healthcare expenses.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Notwithstanding, many parents with whom I have interacted in my Woodgrove division still share their struggles arising from the high cost of maintaining a child, from the purchase of baby formula to enrolling their child to enrichment classes to ensure that the child is ready for school.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They therefore hope that the list of approved uses can be widened to further assist them with these expenses.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Currently, there are restrictions on using CDA funds for optional enrichment programmes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, many of them have confided in me, sharing that while these enrichment programs are offered by the preschool as "optional", they take place during the child's normal curriculum hours and they often feel a great dilemma on whether to enrol their child in these classes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Their primary fear is that their child will lose the learning opportunity and occasion to foster cohesion as well as friendships.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a mother of a five-year-old and one-year-old, I can relate to these concerns they have shared.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Another resident shared that bringing her four children out for family outings is an expensive activity.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: She appreciates our Woodgrove Division's frequent organisation of trips to attractions and places, catering to the needs of family with young children to bond, such as indoor playgrounds and the newly opened Bird Paradise at highly-subsidised rates, as otherwise, she and her husband would either not have been able to bring their children to these places, or would have faced significant financial strain in doing so.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For the sake of Singaporean families, we ought to consider further improving the CDA.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I now move on to the topic of paternity leave.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our paternity leave scheme was introduced more than a decade ago.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The reason why the uptake of paternity leave tends to remain low may likely be due to traditional gender norms and organisational stigma, despite that we are seeing more fathers are stepping up on assuming parenting responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am therefore doubtful that simply by mandating the enhanced paternity leave would encourage a substantive increment in take-up rates, particularly for the shared leave component where it may likely be a situation where couples decide that the wife should take up all 10 weeks so that she can have more time to recuperate both mentally and physically from child birth and enjoy more bonding time with the child during the breastfeeding journey.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I therefore call for the Government to take bolder moves, just as what my Parliamentary colleague, Mr Louis Ng, had sought in his speech earlier, with some of my suggestions as follows.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this regard, the Government can also consider introducing support packages and tax incentives to support employers who encourage their employees to apply for parental leave, providing a workplace culture in which fellow co-workers have a better understanding of the role of the workplace in accepting parents' use of paid leave days.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In Australia, where parents share their childcare benefits at a minimum ratio of 40:60, each parent would be entitled to a "partnership bonus" payment.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the Singaporean context, apart from "Baby Bonus", can we look into providing an extra "New Parents" bonus payout or additional leave entitlement for these young parents where fathers are prepared to step up in utilising their paternity leave to spend quality time in caring for the newborn with their spouses?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We should also be mindful of the gender stereotyping that may occur at the workplace, particularly during the hiring process; a married women in her late 20s or 30s may often be subject and asked by her potential employer on whether she has plans to have children in the near future.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Ultimately, why can we not, as women, excel in both areas – in our careers as well as our role as mothers?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Why must we sacrifice one for the other?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just like what my fellow Parliamentary colleagues, Mr Desmond Choo and Ms Yeo Wan Ling, have shared earlier, I believe that we can and should create a work culture which will afford women the opportunity to achieve a balance and excel in both of these aspects.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These changes in parental schemes in other countries whose demographics and lifestyles are relatable to ours, may allow us to observe the impact of specific policy changes on parental behaviours, and adopt best policies and practices.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Notwithstanding my clarifications and suggestions, I stand in support of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Jessica Tan, do you have a clarification to make?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Maternity leave also involves the recovery of the mother and – in case he does not realise – nine months of carrying a child and then going through childbirth is quite tough.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I hope that he will agree with me that as he advocates for this, he also advocates for time for the mother to recover.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The father having more paternity leave is definitely welcome because then, he can also help to take care of the mother a little bit more as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: If the mother is recovering from childbirth, who is looking after the kid?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Again, for the same reason – as the mothers recover from giving birth to twins or pre-term babies, the fathers need to be there to spend time with the mothers and also look after the children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: So, it is not a zero sum; it is not an either or.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am hoping, again, that we equalise so that both parents can be there for each other and for the children as well.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Although my children are now older and I do not think I will revisit that phase again, I am heartened to see that these changes will benefit future generations of parents.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When my children were born, I was fortunate to be on leave, as I was pursuing my studies, first my degree, then after that my PhD.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This allowed me be fully present during those formative years, allowing my wife to recuperate while I looked after the children together with her – something that I am grateful for to this day.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I did not have to worry about missing and catching up on work although I did have exams and I had multiple assignments to submit as well as reports.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But nothing beats the stigma of taking leave and thinking that your colleagues will take the heavy burden of your work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This Bill by expanding parental leave and supporting working parents will provide similar opportunities for countless families in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It re-affirms our commitment to a society where parents have the time they need to support their children during the crucial early years.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I am grateful that we are moving tin this direction and I look forward t seeing the positive impact these changes will bring to all Singaporean families.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Bill reflects our steadfast commitment to fostering a supportive and inclusive environment for Singapore.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is part of our broader vision to encourage family formation and build a society where parents, regardless of their work situation, can balance family life with professional responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Notably, the introduction of the SPL scheme marks a significant step forward in promoting more equitable caregiving roles for mothers and fathers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We are seeing a growing desire for shared responsibilities in parenting, as we heard earlier, and this Bill empowers both parents to play a proactive role in their child's formative years.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Furthermore, this amendment Bill recognises Singapore's changing work environment.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: One primary concern among SMEs is the potential financial and operational burden these changes may introduce.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: SMEs face unique challenges in maintaining workforce continuity, especially with increased leave entitlements.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Additionally, regular check-ins and a feedback mechanism with SME representatives could help identify implementation challenges early, while temporary financial assistance during the transition period would ease initial burdens.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Training sessions or resource kits would also be valuable, helping smaller businesses understand and implement family-friendly policies effectively.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These measures would enable SMEs to meet their family support obligations without undue strain, balancing their business needs with their contributions to a more family-friendly Singapore.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, Sir, is about addressing workplace stigma associated with parental leave, like I mentioned earlier in my introduction.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Another concern that several parents have shared is the lingering stigma or perception of workplace penalties for those who take extended parental leave.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Despite our progress in building family-friendly workplaces, many parents still feel apprehensive about using their leave entitlements due to fears about career impact.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is especially true for new fathers, who may worry that taking shared leave could signal less commitment to their roles, and for mothers, who may fear that extended leave could limit career opportunities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: While I support the Government's emphasis on protections for employees and penalties for non-compliance, I also hope that we, as a society, can foster a cultural shift that normalises caregiving for both parents.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To address this stigma, I suggest that the Government work closely with NTUC and community organisations such as Dads for Life and Mums for Life to promote a positive culture around parenting.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These organisations have been instrumental in encouraging active parenting, and by partnering with them, we can amplify messages that normalise parental leave for both mothers and fathers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Together, they could develop public campaigns, resources and workplace programmes that highlight the benefits of shared caregiving, fostering a culture where parental responsibilities are seen as integral to a balanced life.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: An increase in childcare leave would greatly support families with greater caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Sufficient leave reduces stress on parents, benefiting their mental health and allowing them to be more present and engaged with their children.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Early childhood is a vital stage of development and a supportive environment promotes mental well-being for both parents and children.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: One approach could be a tiered system that increases leave days based on the number of children, or a pool of flexible family leave days that parents could use as needed.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Expanding childcare leave would further reinforce Singapore's family-friendly framework and support the well-being of all children.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, I would like to highlight several concerns from the community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Recently, M3@Jalan Besar launched the Malay Men's Mental Health Peer Support Group (3MH) a peer support group specifically designed to support the mental health of men in the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Initiatives like this are crucial to ensure that fathers also receive the emotional and mental support that they need for the sake of their families’ well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: By providing a more comprehensive support, we can build a more family-friendly work culture and ensure the mental well-being of parents and children.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: By enhancing parental leave options, expanding eligibility and providing greater financial security for parents, especially those in self-employment or dual employment, we are not only supporting individual families, but also reinforcing the values that underpin our society.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As we look to the future, our policies must continue to evolve with the changing needs of our families and workplaces.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: By promoting family well-being, mental health and inclusivity, these amendments support stronger family bonds and a more resilient society.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These changes will foster stronger family bonds, encourage shared caregiving responsibilities and ultimately, contribute to a more resilient and cohesive society.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It is encouraging that we all agree it is important that we continue to strive towards building an environment that values and supports families and children.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Hany Soh asked if the Government referred to the parental leave provisions in other countries when designing the new SPL scheme.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As I mentioned earlier, the enhancements were developed after studying international practices, and extensive feedback and consultations with parents and the tripartite partners, so that we arrive at a scheme design that best fits our local context.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Members have asked about the eligibility of different groups of parents and the scheme parameters.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Mark Lee asked whether parents with non-traditional work arrangements, such as newly hired employees, will be eligible for the new SPL scheme.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Broadly speaking, working parents who are eligible for the existing parental leave schemes, such as GPML and GPPL will be eligible for the new SPL scheme.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This is a cash benefit-equivalent scheme, similar to the existing GPML and GPPL schemes where parents will receive the cash benefit directly from the Government in lieu of paid leave and can use the cash benefits to make suitable work and caregiving arrangements.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Progressive employers who would like to grant the new SPL to an employee, whose child is born shortly after joining the company and does not meet the minimum employment period of three months, can be reimbursed by the Government if the employee has met all other eligibility criteria.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The leave that is voluntarily granted by the employer should also follow the conditions of the new SPL scheme, such as being taken within 12 months of the child's birth.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Hany Soh asked if there is flexibility to the new requirement for employees to provide at least four weeks' notice before commencing parental leave in instances of pre-mature births.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Mark Lee also asked if operational constraints would serve as reasonable cause for an employer to delay the granting of the new SPL scheme.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I wish to highlight that the consumption period for the new SPL is 12 months from the child's date of birth, and this provides a reasonable window within which the leave can be taken.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As demonstrated by the examples raised by Ms Hany Soh and Mr Mark Lee, this is indeed why it is important for employers and employees to have early conversations and plan ahead as soon as possible so that a suitable leave arrangement can be worked out to meet the needs of both parties.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This could include taking the leave more flexibly in weeks, days, or half-days, as was mentioned by Ms Mariam Jaafar, over the 12 months, to avoid peak periods or periods of manpower shortage, or to meet changes in parents' caregiving circumstances.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Louis Chua asked whether we can extend the consumption period for the new SPL scheme.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: When developing the new shared parental leave scheme in consultation with the tripartite partners, we had considered allowing parents more flexibility to take the new SPL over a longer period of two years.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, employers preferred a shorter consumption period to reduce the uncertainty on when employees may be absent from work, which could result in greater challenges in making manpower arrangements.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We are always mindful that we have to balance employers' needs, even as we try our best to support new parents.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Taking indeed all these considerations, we decided on a consumption period of 12 months, which is also aligned with that for our maternity and paternity leave schemes.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Several Members called on greater support for self-employed persons and sought clarifications on the reimbursement of parental leave for those with multiple employers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Jean See asked whether the Tripartite Standard on Contracting with Self-employed Persons could state upfront that if the contracted freelancer must absent herself due to pregnancy and childbirth, the service buyer should consider substitution options rather than to terminate the contract.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Tripartite Standard on Contracting with Self-employed Persons states that when a self-employed person enters into an agreement with a service-buyer, the parties’ obligations and how the agreement may be varied, among other things, should be set out clearly in writing.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I encourage self-employed persons and service buyers to negotiate contracts that are mutually favourable, including providing for absences due to pregnancy and childbirth.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Prescribing that the service buyer must consider substitution options when a self-employed person absents herself due to pregnancy and childbirth may make it very rigid for service buyers who may have legitimate urgent business needs.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Jean See also sought assurance that the Government will not condone pregnancy discrimination if a freelancer approaches the TAFEP or the Small Claims Tribunal about losing a contract or contracted gig after disclosing her pregnancy status to the client.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I wish to assure Ms See that in the final report of the Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness, the Committee recommended including additional guidelines in the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices (TGFEP) to provide greater clarity that corporate service buyers and intermediaries should not discriminate based on characteristics that are not related to the job.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: MOM will work with the tripartite partners to include these additional guidelines in the TGFEP.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Jean See also asked if GPML can be paid to eligible freelancers when the maternity leave commences and not after the ninth week of the maternity leave period.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I wish to clarify that under the Employment Act and CDCA, the first eight weeks of maternity leave for the mother’s first two child orders are paid for by the employer and the Government reimburses for the last eight weeks.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Freelancers are considered self-employed and the same approach is adopted for self-employed persons.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The first eight weeks of maternity leave for the first two child orders are also paid for by the self-employed person, while the Government pays for the lost income for the ninth to 16th week of maternity leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: To ensure accountability for the use of public funds, paying on a reimbursement basis is a safeguard to ensure that the leave is taken as intended before payment is released.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, we do understand that cash flow may be an important consideration for freelancers and self-employed persons.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: To mitigate this, self-employed persons are encouraged to submit their claims accurately as soon as possible.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Claim submissions that are accurate and complete will typically be reimbursed within 10 working days.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Self-employed persons can also claim reimbursement for any portion of Government-paid leave that has been taken even when there is still remaining leave to be consumed.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This means self-employed persons can submit claims between the ninth and 16th week of maternity leave for the first two child orders and need not wait for the period of eight weeks to have passed before claiming for reimbursement.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Jean See and Mr Mark Lee asked how the reimbursement limit will apply for parents who have multiple employments, such as those who hold multiple jobs, or are both an employee and a self-employed person.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Such parents will be able to take parental leave with each employer as well as take time-off as a self-employed person.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Where there are multiple employers and the total claim amount exceeds the reimbursement limit, the reimbursement for each employer will be further determined based on the proportion of the employer’s claim out of the total claim amount submitted by all employers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We encourage employees to inform their employers before consuming the leave, if they have multiple employers and are likely to exceed the reimbursement limit.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I wish to assure Mr Mark Lee and Mr Melvin Yong that these details will be covered in the guidelines which MSF will provide on its website.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: To Mr Mark Lee’s question on the computation of income for self-employed persons, it is based on the income set out in the individual’s Notice of Assessment and should therefore cover any seasonal variations within a year.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Louis Ng asked how we can encourage fathers, especially low-income fathers, to take more paternity leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Hany Soh also suggested incentivising fathers to take more leave by introducing additional bonuses, either in the form of payouts or additional leave to couples if the father takes paternity leave or shares a certain portion of the new SPL scheme.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Louis Chua suggested making the reimbursement for a portion of paternity leave contingent on fathers taking a minimum number of weeks of leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: First, this is why we are introducing new employment protection for fathers taking GPPL.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mothers are currently protected against dismissals when they are on maternity leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: By extending the same protection to fathers who are on paternity leave, we want to send a strong signal to employers that it is important for them to also support their male employees to take parental leave, besides their female employees.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We hope that this protection will provide fathers with the assurance and peace of mind to go ahead to use their paternity leave entitlement.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The same protection will also be extended to employees taking adoption leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I agree with Ms Mariam Jaafar and Ms Hany Soh that we must continue to strengthen protection against discrimination of women with childbearing intentions and parents at the workplace and the upcoming Workplace Fairness Bill will address this.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: On the new protections, Mr Desmond Choo asked to increase the penalty for employers who are first-time offenders, from the current fine not exceeding $5,000 to a fine not exceeding $10,000.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The current penalties under the CDCA are in line with other employment offences for statutory leave provisions in the Employment Act and we will take the Member’s feedback into consideration when reviewing the penalties.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It is also important to understand the spirit of the law, which is to encourage a supportive workplace environment for families.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Members have provided useful suggestions, and we will continue to review our parental leave schemes and study how we can design them better to encourage utilisation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This brings me to my second point that beyond legislation and Government support, workplace culture and societal norms are key factors that influence whether parents use their parental leave entitlements.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I echo Mr Desmond Choo, Ms Mariam Jaafar and Dr Wan Rizal, who highlighted that a shift in policy cannot by itself drive cultural change.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Encouraging greater paternal involvement and shared parental responsibilities require mindset shifts in our society.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Workplaces with supportive supervisors and coworkers can make a huge difference to assure fathers to go ahead and take leave to bond with and care for their newborns.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Therefore, the Government has been, and will continue to work with tripartite partners and community partners such as Families for Life Council and Centre for Fathering to encourage employers to foster family-friendly workplaces.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I urge supervisors to be supportive when their employees apply for paternity leave and hope that co-workers will be understanding and help to cover their colleagues who take time off work to care for their children.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I also call on parents to be ready to extend similar support when they return to work, should their colleagues also need to take time off from work to tend to their families.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As Ms Mariam Jaafar highlighted, we will continue to track our progress and the take up of our parental leave schemes.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: MSF published the "Family Trends Report" in July 2024, which provides key annual updates on Singapore’s family trends as we work towards achieving a Singapore Made for Families.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The report includes the utilisation trends of Government-paid Leave Schemes.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The National Population and Talent Division also regularly conducts the Marriage and Parenthood Survey to understand perceptions toward marriage and parenthood, including that of parental caregiving roles and the actual division of childcare duties at home between men and women.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Several Members have also called for further increases in parental leave provisions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about further increasing paternity leave to eventually equalise maternity and paternity leave, so that we avoid entrenching gender stereotypes.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Maternity leave is longer than paternity leave, given that mothers need time to recuperate physically after childbirth, a point which was emphasised by Member Ms Jessica Tan earlier.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Although the duration of maternity and paternity leave differs, the Government has been mindful about the importance of encouraging shared parental responsibility.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: And you can see, from the progressive rounds of enhancements in recent years, that they have focused mainly on increasing paternity leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Louis Chua, Ms Mariam Jaafar and Dr Wan Rizal suggested increasing Childcare Leave, including to tier it according to the number of children or combining it into a pool of family leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Previously, all preschools were already allowed to close 7.5 days per year – six closure days and three half-days on the eves of selected public holidays.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We fully recognise that caring for a child is a long-term commitment and that working parents must continue to manage their work and caregiving responsibilities even after the first year of the child’s life.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Currently, each working parent whose youngest child is below seven years old is entitled to six days of Childcare Leave per year.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: A working couple would therefore have a total of 12 days of Childcare Leave on top of their annual leave provisions, which they can use for preschool closure days and other childcare purposes.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Any further enhancements to our leave schemes will require us to strike a fine balance between the caregiving needs of parents and the manpower and operational needs of employers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We also need to provide employers with some time to adjust to the significant increases in overall parental leave provisions with the introduction of the new SPL scheme.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Nevertheless, we will continue to regularly review our leave policies in consultation with parents and the tripartite partners.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Beyond legislated leave provisions, we encourage other sustainable ways that support parents and other caregivers in juggling work and caregiving commitments, such as FWAs.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Tripartite Guidelines on Flexible Workplace Arrangement Requests will take effect from 1 December 2024 and the mandatory guidelines will enable employers and employees to have open discussions and work out arrangements that can meet both parties’ needs.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We should focus on building confidence and capabilities among companies to manage flexible workplace arrangements effectively, instead of relying on legislation alone.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We thank the NTUC's efforts on this front.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Even as some Members call for even more leave provisions, other Members have highlighted the potential challenges that businesses may face in managing the extended absences of employees.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Mark Lee, Ms Hany Soh, Ms Hazel Poa, Dr Wan Rizal and Ms Yeo Wan Ling have called for better support to help companies, especially SMEs, with manpower and operational constraints.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We fully understand that employers are concerned about the impact of the parental leave enhancements on their business and manpower arrangements.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As I mentioned in my opening speech, we have therefore worked closely with tripartite partners and employer representatives, to design the parental leave enhancements in a way that best mitigates some of the challenges that employers may face.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This fully covers the wages of the majority of employees on leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Employers can use the wage savings to mitigate the operational impact of their employees going on leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This includes, hiring and training temporary workers, providing additional remuneration to recognise the effort of colleagues covering for the employees on leave and supporting any overlapping periods for handovers when re-integrating returning employees.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For example, in response to feedback, we have since allowed claims for childcare leave to be submitted in batches, instead of individually, to reduce the administrative burden on employers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We will continue to review and improve our reimbursement processes to support employers in providing parental leave.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For the longer term, we encourage employers to take this opportunity to strengthen their manpower planning capabilities and make operational and system adjustments.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: After all, given the demographic challenges of a declining birth rate and an ageing workforce, mature economies and societies like ours must increasingly find ways to effectively navigate manpower constraints in future and manage a more flexible workforce well.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Employers can tap on existing grants and resources, such as the Productivity Solutions Grant, to improve business productivity and automation and implement FWAs or use SkillsFuture Credits for their HR professionals to obtain the Institute for Human Resources Professionals' certifications and be equipped with progressive people practices.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked whether the Government can consider extending the Shared Parental Benefits to couples whose babies are expected to be born in the first-quarter of 2025.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I seek Members' understanding that specific start dates are required for any new measure or enhancement, to ensure a smooth implementation process for all stakeholders involved.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This start date applies to both the SPL scheme as well as its cash benefit-equivalent Shared Parental Benefits scheme.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Hazel Poa spoke about other concerns that we must also address to build a conducive environment for families.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In the infographic I distributed earlier, Members will see how the Government has put in place a comprehensive suite of support measures across various domains, such as housing, healthcare and education, and we will continue to review our measures to address the needs of parents.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Hany Soh asked if we could further enhance the CDA to cover optional enrichment programmes and family outings.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The CDA is intended to help parents defray healthcare and educational costs and we have scoped the use of the CDA accordingly.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We regularly review the uses of CDA and will take Ms Soh's feedback into consideration.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, in his National Day Rally speech, had also said that the Government is looking into ways to provide more support to larger families with three or more children, such as the resident, whom Ms Hany Soh mentioned.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Melvin Yong suggested further healthcare support for mothers, such as through providing universal maternity insurance for all mothers-to-be, including those with pre-existing conditions to allay worries about unexpected pregnancy complications.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I wish to highlight that as a universal health insurance scheme, MediShield Life covers all Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents, including mothers-to-be with pre-existing conditions, for life.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: They can be assured that MediShield Life covers the treatment of serious pregnancy and delivery-related complications.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For general maternity expenses, the Government provides subsidies of up to 80% and allows the use MediSave through the MediSave Maternity Package.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Expectant mothers may choose to purchase maternity insurance policies for added coverage.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Such maternity insurance plans are optional private products, where the benefits and terms and conditions are determined by insurers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I am grateful for the views shared by the Members and thank them for their various suggestions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, we have made much progress since.      .
